1:4.t: The province of Asia: see Acts 2:9. "The seven spirits": perhaps the Holy Spirit in His fullness (compare Isaiah 11:2), or seven angelic spirits before God's throne.

1:5.t: "Loves us": the KJV's "loved us"; many early manuscripts read "loves". "Washed us": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "freed us".

1:6.t: "Kings and priests": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "a kingdom and priests". Echoes Exodus 19:6.

1:8.t: "The Beginning and the End": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here.
"Alpha and Omega": the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. God is the beginning and end of all things. In 22:13 Jesus applies the title to Himself.

1:9.t: Patmos was a small island in the Aegean Sea, used by the Romans as a place of exile.

1:10.t: "The Lord's Day": Sunday, the day of the resurrection (see 1 Corinthians 16:2).

1:11.t: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here. "Pergamum": the KJV's "Pergamos".

2:6.t: The Nicolaitans are not otherwise known; they apparently taught that Christians could join in pagan feasts and immorality (compare 2:14-15).

2:13.t: "Where Satan has his throne": the KJV's "where Satan's seat is". Pergamum was a center of emperor worship and had a great altar of Zeus.

2:20.t: Jezebel: a name borrowed from the wicked queen of 1 Kings 16:31 and 21:25, given to a false prophetess in Thyatira.

2:23.t: "Hearts and minds": the KJV's "reins and hearts", the kidneys and heart, the seat of thought and feeling.

3:14.t: Laodicea was a wealthy banking city with a medical school known for eye salve (3:18). Its water came from hot springs by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm.

4:3.t: "Carnelian": the KJV's "sardine stone", a reddish gem.

4:6.t: "Living creatures": the KJV's "beasts"; Greek zoa. Compare the creatures of Ezekiel 1:5-14 and the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-3.

4:8.t: "Holy, holy, holy": the threefold "holy" of Isaiah 6:3, emphasizing God's complete holiness.

4:11.t: "O Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "our Lord and God". "They exist": the KJV's "for thy pleasure they are"; the Greek dia to thelema sou means "by Your will".

5:1.t: "Scroll": the KJV's "book". Books were then written on scrolls.

5:9.t: "Us": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "people" or "them". 5:10 "Us ... we": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "them ... they". "Kings and priests": see 1:6.

6:6.t: "About a liter ... about three liters": the KJV's "a measure ... three measures"; Greek choinix, about a liter, a day's ration. "A denarius": the KJV's "a penny", a day's wage. These were famine prices.

7:4.t: "144,000": the KJV's "an hundred and forty and four thousand".

"144,000 ... a great multitude that no one could count": readers understand the 144,000 as Jewish believers, as the whole church pictured as the true Israel (the same group as the great multitude), or as a special group of martyrs. Twelve times twelve times a thousand suggests the complete people of God.

7:5.t: Dan is missing from the list, perhaps because of its early idolatry (Judges 18:30), and Joseph and Manasseh are both listed. Names follow the Old Testament spelling: Judah, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Zebulun.

8:11.t: Wormwood is a bitter plant (compare Jeremiah 9:15).

8:13.t: "An angel": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "an eagle".

9:16.t: "Two hundred million": the KJV's "two hundred thousand thousand", a number meant to overwhelm.

10:6.t: "There will be time no longer": the KJV's reading; the Greek means "there will be no more delay".

11:2.t: "Forty-two months ... 1,260 days": both are three and a half years, a period from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7. "1,260": the KJV's "a thousand two hundred and threescore".

11:8.t: "Our Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "their Lord".

11:17.t: "And who is to come": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

12:14.t: "A time, times and half a time": three and a half years (Daniel 7:25, 12:7).

12:17.t: "Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read only "Jesus".

13:1.t: "I stood": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "he stood", meaning the dragon, and place these words at the end of 12:17. "A blasphemous name": the KJV's "the name of blasphemy"; many manuscripts read "names".

13:2.t: Compare the four beasts of Daniel 7:3-7.

13:8.t: "Slain from the creation of the world": the Greek can also be read "whose names have not been written from the creation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain" (compare 17:8).

13:18.t: "666": the KJV's "Six hundred threescore and six"; some early manuscripts read "616".

"The number of the beast ... 666": many take it as gematria, the practice of adding the numerical values of letters in a name. The Hebrew letters of "Nero Caesar" add up to 666 (and a variant spelling to 616). Others take six, falling short of the perfect seven, as a symbol of complete imperfection and evil.

14:1.t: "His Father's name": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "His name and His Father's name".

14:8.t: "Babylon": a code name for Rome, or for any human power opposed to God. Echoes Isaiah 21:9.

14:20.t: "About 300 kilometers": the KJV's "a thousand and six hundred furlongs".

15:3.t: "King of the saints": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "King of the nations".
"The song of Moses ... and of the Lamb": recalling Exodus 15, Israel's song after crossing the Red Sea. The new exodus through Christ echoes the first.

15:6.t: "Linen": the KJV's reading; some manuscripts read "stone".

16:5.t: "And who shall be": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the Holy One".

16:13.t: "The false prophet": the second beast of 13:11-17.

16:16.t: "Armageddon": Hebrew Har Megiddo, "Mount of Megiddo". Megiddo overlooked a plain where many decisive battles were fought (Judges 5:19, 2 Kings 23:29).

16:21.t: "About 34 kilograms": the KJV's "about the weight of a talent".

17:9.t: "Seven hills": the KJV's "seven mountains". Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

18:12.t: "Citron wood": the KJV's "thyine wood", a fragrant wood prized for furniture.

18:13.t: "Human beings sold as slaves": the KJV's "slaves, and souls of men".

19:1.t: "Hallelujah": the KJV's "Alleluia", Hebrew for "Praise the LORD". This chapter is the only place the word appears in the New Testament.

19:13.t: "Dipped in blood": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts read "sprinkled with blood".
"The Word of God" (Greek ho logos tou theou): see John 1:1.

20:1.t: "A thousand years" (Latin millennium): Christians have long held three main views. Premillennialists expect Christ to return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth; postmillennialists expect Christ to return after a long era of the gospel's triumph; amillennialists understand the thousand years as the present age between Christ's first and second comings, in which He reigns and Satan is restrained. The chapter's purpose is to assure the faithful of their vindication and of Satan's final defeat.

20:8.t: Gog and Magog: see Ezekiel 38-39, where they are enemies of God's people from the north.

20:12.t: "Before God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "before the throne".

21:16.t: "About 2,200 kilometers": the KJV's "twelve thousand furlongs". The city is a perfect cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20).

21:17.t: "About 65 meters": the KJV's "an hundred and forty and four cubits", perhaps the height or the thickness of the wall.

21:19.t: The identification of some ancient gem names is uncertain. "Agate ... onyx ... ruby ... turquoise": the KJV's "chalcedony ... sardonyx ... sardius ... chrysoprasus". Compare the twelve stones of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20).

21:24.t: "Of those who are saved": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

22:14.t: "Do His commandments": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "wash their robes".

22:19.t: "The book of life": the KJV's reading. Nearly all Greek manuscripts read "the tree of life". The KJV followed Erasmus's Greek text, which here was translated back from Latin.

22:21.t: "With you all": the KJV's reading; manuscripts differ, some reading "with all God's people".

1:1.t: "Revelation" (Greek apokalypsis): an unveiling, the source of the name "Apocalypse". "Of Jesus Christ" can mean a revelation from Him, about Him, or both.

1:20.t: "Angels" (Greek angeloi): messengers. Readers understand them as guardian angels of the churches, or as human messengers or leaders.

2:7.t: "The one who is victorious" (Greek ho nikon): the KJV's "him that overcometh". Each of the seven letters ends with a promise to the one who conquers. See John 16:33.

2:11.t: "The second death": final judgment, the lake of fire (20:14).

3:20.t: "I stand at the door and knock": spoken to a church, but often applied to each person's invitation to Christ.

5:6.t: "A Lamb, looking as if it had been slain": John is told of a Lion (5:5) and sees a Lamb. Christ conquers by His sacrificial death. "Lamb" (Greek arnion) is John's main name for Christ in Revelation, used twenty-nine times. "Seven horns and seven eyes": complete power and complete knowledge.

7:14.t: "The great tribulation" (Greek tes thlipseos tes megales): see Matthew 24:21. Christians differ on whether it is a final period before Christ's return or describes the suffering of God's people throughout the age.

8:1.t: The seven trumpets, like the seven seals before them and the seven bowls after (chapters 15-16), describe God's judgments. Christians read Revelation in different ways: as events of John's own day (preterist), as the course of church history (historicist), as events still to come before Christ's return (futurist), or as pictures of the ongoing conflict between God and evil throughout the age (idealist). Many combine these approaches.

11:7.t: "The beast" (Greek therion): a wild animal, introduced fully in chapter 13.

11:15.t: "Christ" (Greek christos): God's Anointed. See Matthew 1:1. Compare Psalm 2:2.

12:1.t: The woman is understood as Israel giving birth to the Messiah, as the people of God in both covenants, or, in some traditions, as Mary. The male child is Christ (12:5, quoting Psalm 2:9).

12:9.t: "That ancient serpent ... the devil, or Satan": connects the dragon with the serpent of Genesis 3. "Devil" (Greek diabolos) means "slanderer"; "Satan" (Hebrew satan) means "accuser" (12:10). See Zechariah 3:1.

14:4.t: "Virgins" (Greek parthenoi): probably a picture of spiritual purity, faithfulness to the Lamb rather than idolatry, which the prophets called adultery.

14:10.t: "Tormented ... forever and ever": see the note at 2 Thessalonians 1:9.

14:14.t: Two harvests: the grain harvest, perhaps the gathering of God's people, and the grape harvest of judgment (compare Joel 3:13, Isaiah 63:1-6).

16:15.t: "I come like a thief": Christ's words break into the vision (compare 3:3, Matthew 24:43).

17:1.t: "Babylon the Great": the ancient enemy of God's people becomes a symbol of human power, wealth and seduction opposed to God, for John's first readers almost certainly the city of Rome. The great prostitute stands in contrast to the bride of the Lamb (19:7, 21:2).

17:14.t: "Lord of lords and King of kings": a title of supreme rule (compare Deuteronomy 10:17, 1 Timothy 6:15), given here to the Lamb.

19:7.t: "The wedding of the Lamb": the church as Christ's bride (compare Ephesians 5:25-27). Her clothing is "the righteous acts of God's holy people", given her as a gift ("was given her").

20:14.t: "The second death": final judgment, separation from God. See 2:11.

21:1.t: "No longer any sea": the sea in the Bible often stands for chaos, danger and evil (13:1). The new creation will be free of them.

21:3.t: "Dwelling place" (Greek skene): the KJV's "tabernacle", the tent where God lived among Israel. See John 1:14. The goal of the whole Bible is fulfilled: God living with His people.

22:13.t: "The Alpha and the Omega": Jesus claims the title God used of Himself in 1:8 and 21:6.

22:16.t: "The Root and the Offspring of David": compare Isaiah 11:1, 10. "The bright Morning Star": compare Numbers 24:17 and 2 Peter 1:19.

22:20.t: "Come, Lord Jesus" (Greek erchou kyrie Iesou): the prayer behind the Aramaic Maranatha (1 Corinthians 16:22). The Bible ends with the promise of Christ's coming and the church's answering prayer.
